common_name: Vesta Nerine (Large Pale Pink Hardy Guernsey Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck just at or slightly above soil level in spring (or very late summer in mild climates), in sharply drained, lean soil in full sun against a warm wall or border edge.

directions: Plant bulbs with their necks just at or slightly above soil level in a warm, sheltered spot with sharply drained soil, since Nerine bowdenii resents wet winter conditions around its neck. Vesta sends up leafless stalks in early autumn topped with rounded umbels of soft, clear pink, faintly fragrant flowers with gently waved and recurved petal tips, followed by strap-shaped leaves that persist through winter and die back by summer. A deep, dry mulch over the dormant bulbs helps protect them through hard winters at the cold end of the range, and clumps left undisturbed for several years flower far more freely than recently divided ones. Site it along a south-facing wall or border edge where the summer heat that triggers reliable autumn bloom is most assured.

planting.note: Plant dormant bulbs in late summer or early fall with the neck exposed above the compost line, in a gritty, sharply drained mix in full sun.

directions: Pot up dormant bulbs in late summer with the neck exposed above the compost line, using a gritty, free-draining mix, and grow in a bright, frost-free spot through the flowering and leaf-growth season. Stephanie produces sturdy stems topped with rounded heads of soft pale pink, crystalline-textured flowers in autumn, ahead of the strappy foliage that follows and persists through winter and spring. Water sparingly once the leaves begin to yellow in late spring and keep the bulb completely dry through summer dormancy, since overwatering a resting sarniensis bulb is the most common cause of failure to rebloom. Where winters stay reliably above freezing, bulbs can instead be grown outdoors in a raised, sun-baked bed against a warm wall.

planting.note: Plant small bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level, in gritty, humus-poor, fast-draining soil, siting them where they get at least half a day of sun.

directions: Plant the small bulbs with their necks at soil level in a gritty, fast-draining mix, siting them where they get several hours of direct sun a day; in their native fynbos they often flower most heavily on rocky slopes recently cleared by fire. Slender leafless stems appear in autumn carrying small umbels of a few crenulated, pale-to-deep-pink flowers, followed by narrow leaves that persist through the cooler months and die back as the ground dries in late spring. Keep bulbs completely dry through their summer dormancy to replicate the winter-rainfall climate of the Cape, growing them in pots that can be moved under cover wherever summer rain is unavoidable. Being one of the smallest garden nerine species, it suits trough and rock-garden culture among other Cape bulbs more than mass border planting.

planting.note: Plant corms about three inches deep after all frost danger passes and soil has warmed, in humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade to morning sun.

directions: Plant corms about three inches deep in humus-rich, well-drained soil after the danger of frost has passed, siting them in dappled shade or morning sun that mimics the seasonally dry tropical woodland this Mexican species grows in naturally. Unlike its upright, brightly spotted relative Tigridia pavonia, meleagris carries its blossoms facing downward on a single wiry stem, their checkered maroon-and-cream pattern echoing a woodland fritillary rather than a tiger lily, above one solitary pleated leaf. Water regularly through the summer bloom period, then withhold water and lift corms for frost-free winter storage anywhere the ground freezes. Its unusual nodding habit and mottled coloring make it a conversation-piece addition to a shaded bulb collection rather than a border mass-planting subject.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant corms after all frost danger passes and soil has warmed, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to very light shade.

directions: Plant corms in spring once the soil has warmed, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to very light shade, allowing extra room since this species grows taller and sturdier than the more commonly grown Tigridia pavonia. Wiry stems carry a succession of large, deep red flowers boldly spotted in yellow, held upright and outward-facing, with each individual bloom lasting only a day before the next opens. Because it hails from cool, high-elevation Mexican meadows, it tolerates a longer, milder growing season than lowland Tigridia species and appreciates a slightly cooler root run in hot-summer gardens. Lift and store corms over winter wherever the ground freezes, replanting once night temperatures stay reliably above the mid-50s.

common_name: Nani Pineapple Lily (Soft Pink Fragrant Aloha Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs about three inches deep once the soil has warmed, in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; Nani is part of the compact Aloha Lily breeding series derived from Eucomis vandermerwei and zambesiaca.

directions: Plant bulbs about three inches deep once the soil has warmed, in rich, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing them to allow the compact rosette of glossy foliage room to fill out. Nani is part of the Aloha Lily breeding series developed from Eucomis vandermerwei and zambesiaca parentage, producing dense spikes of soft, sweetly fragrant pink flowers topped with the tuft of leafy bracts that gives pineapple lilies their common name. Its scent and compact habit make it especially rewarding near patios and containers where the fragrance can be appreciated up close, unlike many larger, unscented Eucomis comosa selections. Reduce watering as the foliage yellows in fall and store bulbs dry over winter in climates colder than its hardiness range.

common_name: Maui Pineapple Lily (Pure White Aloha Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs about three inches deep once the soil has warmed, in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; Maui is a pure white-flowered member of the compact Aloha Lily breeding series.

directions: Plant bulbs roughly three inches deep in rich, well-drained soil once the soil has warmed, giving Maui full sun to bring out its densely packed spikes of pure white, gently fragrant flowers, a rarer color among pineapple lily hybrids that tend toward pink, burgundy, or green. As part of the compact Aloha Lily breeding series, it forms a tidy clump well suited to containers and border fronts rather than the taller, sprawling habit of straight Eucomis comosa. Keep soil evenly moist through summer bloom, then taper off watering as leaves yellow in autumn and store bulbs dry over winter outside its hardiness range. Established clumps resent frequent disturbance and flower most heavily when left in place for several years.

planting.note: Plant bulbs about three inches deep once the soil has warmed, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Kona is an Aloha Lily series selection noted for producing multiple flower spikes per bulb.

directions: Plant bulbs about three inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil once the soil has warmed in spring, siting Kona in full sun where its unusually heavy flowering can be fully appreciated. This Aloha Lily series selection produces four to six pineapple-shaped flower spikes per bulb over a single summer, each packed with small starry florets, giving a longer and showier bloom display than many single-spike pineapple lily types. Water regularly during active summer growth and flowering, then reduce watering as foliage yellows in fall ahead of winter dormancy. Divide congested clumps only occasionally, since eucomis bulbs generally reward being left undisturbed for several seasons between divisions.

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in consistently moist, well-drained soil in full sun; unlike many drought-tolerant fynbos watsonias, this streamside species does not tolerate full dry-summer dormancy.

directions: Plant corms in a consistently moist, well-drained site that mimics the streamside habitat this rare southern Cape species grows in naturally, since unlike many drought-tolerant fynbos watsonias it does not tolerate a fully dry summer dormancy. Tall, wiry spikes rise well above the sword-shaped foliage from late summer into fall, carrying an unusually short-tubed flower ranging from red-orange to mauve-pink depending on the population. Site it along a pond margin, streamside border, or anywhere soil stays reliably damp through the growing season, and mulch corms for winter protection at the colder end of its range. Because wild populations are restricted to just a couple of mountain ranges, seek out nursery-propagated stock rather than wild-collected corms.
sources: SANBI Red List of South African Plants

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in lean, fast-draining sandy or sandstone-derived soil in full sun; give a winter-wet, summer-dry cycle matching its native fynbos habitat.

directions: Plant corms in lean, fast-draining sandy or sandstone-derived soil in full sun, giving this smaller fynbos watsonia the winter-wet, summer-dry cycle it experiences on its native Cape slopes. Wiry spikes carry glossy, sword-shaped leaves about half the height of the flowering stem and showy blooms that vary considerably between wild populations, from pink and purple to orange or white, opening in spring. Keep soil evenly moist through the winter and spring growing season, then withhold water completely once foliage yellows to replicate its natural summer dormancy. Its compact stature compared to the larger border watsonias suits rock gardens and raised beds where good drainage can be guaranteed.
sources: SANBI Red List of South African Plants

common_name: Auriculata Harlequin Flower (Cream and Deep Yellow Sparaxis)

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun in zones 8-10; requires a dry summer dormancy.

directions: Plant corms in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun, giving this rare Cape species the winter-wet, summer-baked cycle of its native sandstone slopes near the Gifberg and Matsikamma mountains. Unscented flowers open in late winter with a pale mauve dorsal petal set above deep yellow lower petals that fade to cream, the throat marked with grey-purple, a color combination quite distinct from the red-and-black patterning of the widely grown Sparaxis tricolor hybrids. Distinctive leaves with a thickened, vein-lined margin and purple-speckled sheaths help distinguish it from closely related Cape sparaxis species even before it flowers. Because it is known from only a handful of wild locations, grow nursery-propagated corms and let the foliage die back completely before lifting or dividing clumps.

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in lean, fast-draining sandy or rocky soil in full sun in zones 8-10; requires a dry summer dormancy.

directions: Plant corms in lean, fast-draining sandy or rocky soil in full sun, providing the dry-summer, wet-winter cycle typical of its native sandstone habitat in the Northern and Western Cape. This compact species produces unscented, bilaterally symmetrical flowers in late summer, colored purple with bold white spade-shaped markings on the lower petals, a pattern once considered a form of the more widespread Sparaxis variegata before being recognized as its own species. Water through the winter and spring growing season and allow the corms to dry off completely as the foliage yellows in early summer. Its small stature and short flowering window make it best suited to a dedicated bulb frame, trough, or rock garden rather than a general mixed border.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun in zones 8-10; requires a dry summer dormancy.

directions: Plant corms in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun, in a spot that stays dry through summer to match the winter-rainfall climate of the western Cape forelands this species inhabits from the Cape Peninsula north to the Olifants River Valley. Compared to showier garden sparaxis hybrids, its flowers are noticeably smaller, with an erect to slightly hooded upper petal held well above a shorter, contrastingly yellow lower petal. Water regularly from fall through spring while the narrow leaves are actively growing, then stop entirely once the foliage begins to yellow and die back for summer dormancy. Its diminutive scale and understated coloring make it a specialty choice for Cape-bulb collectors rather than a mainstream bedding subject.
